front_blocks.md: Why is cisplatin medically active while transplatin is not?

back_blocks.md: Cisplatin is **polar** because the two electronegative Cl ligands are on the same side, creating a charge imbalance that allows it to bind to DNA. Transplatin is **non-polar** because the ligands are opposite each other, so the charges cancel.

front_blocks.md: Octahedral complexes with three identical bidentate ligands can exhibit optical isomerism.

back_blocks.md: **True.** Such complexes have no plane of symmetry and exist as non-superimposable mirror images — the defining feature of **optical isomers**.

front_blocks.md: What structural feature allows octahedral complexes to display cis-trans isomerism?

back_blocks.md: An octahedral complex displays cis-trans isomerism when it has **two ligands that are different** from the other four. These two different ligands can be either adjacent (cis) or opposite (trans).

front_blocks.md: Why is the cis isomer of [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> polar?

back_blocks.md: In the cis isomer, the two H<sub>2</sub>O ligands are on the same side. The oxygen atoms in water are more electronegative than the nitrogen atoms in NH<sub>3</sub>, creating a partial negative charge on one side and making the complex **polar**.
